pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Your handler ends with `go sendConfirmation(order)`. Name three things that go wrong with that, and what a job queue gives you instead.
expected_points: the goroutine dies with the process — deploy, crash, OOM — and the work is gone with no record
no retry and no visibility: a failed send leaves nothing to query, count or alert on
unbounded concurrency under load, so no backpressure on the dependency
the request context is cancelled when the handler returns, so anything using it stops mid-flight
a queue is durability plus a retry policy plus a concurrency limit

questions.prompt: Why is `tx.Commit()` followed by `queue.Publish(job)` unsafe, and why is swapping the two no better? What does the transactional outbox do about it?
expected_points: a crash between the two loses the job silently — nothing failed, nothing retried, nothing logged
publishing first can leave a phantom job for a row whose transaction rolled back
two systems cannot be committed atomically, so no ordering is safe
write the job into the same database in the same transaction as the data that justifies it — both or neither
when the job must reach a broker, a relay publishes committed outbox rows, and may republish after a crash

questions.prompt: Why is delivery at least once rather than exactly once, and what does that force the consumer to do?
expected_points: there is a gap between the effect happening and the queue recording it; a crash in that gap causes redelivery
no transaction spans your database and someone else's system, so the gap cannot be closed in general
the consumer must be idempotent: running the job twice has the effect of running it once
keyed on the job id — a dedup ledger inserted in the same transaction as the effect, or a naturally idempotent write, or the third party's idempotency key
exactly-once effect is achievable; exactly-once delivery is not

questions.prompt: In the exercise, `MarkProcessed` runs in the same transaction as the handler's work rather than in a transaction of its own that commits first. Why does that matter, and what breaks if you mark the job processed and commit before the handler runs?
expected_points: the effect and the record of the effect must commit together, or the queue's knowledge disagrees with reality
a marker written outside would survive a failed attempt, so the retry would skip the work it is retrying — silent loss
on rollback the marker disappears with the effect, so the retry is a real retry
a redelivery of committed work sees the marker, skips the handler and still finishes the job

questions.prompt: Describe the retry policy you implemented: backoff, jitter, and when a job stops being retried.
expected_points: exponential: base doubled per attempt, capped at a maximum
jitter randomises each delay so jobs that failed together do not retry together and re-create the outage
the randomness is injected so the policy is testable, like the clock
a bounded attempt budget, after which the job is dead-lettered with its cause kept for a human
an error wrapping ErrPermanent skips the budget entirely — no retry fixes a deleted record or an unparseable payload

questions.prompt: What exactly does graceful shutdown of the worker pool do, why does the in-flight job need `context.WithoutCancel`, and why is shutdown still not what makes the system correct?
expected_points: stop claiming new jobs, finish the ones already claimed, then return
a claimed job that inherits the cancellation fails halfway, turning every deploy into a pile of retries
WithoutCancel keeps the values and drops the cancellation; production bounds the drain with a timeout
the lease is what makes a hard kill survivable — shutdown is politeness, redelivery is the guarantee

questions.prompt: A worker holds a 30-second lease and its handler takes 45 seconds. What happens, and what are your options?
expected_points: the lease expires and another worker claims the job while the first is still running it
the job runs twice concurrently, which is exactly the case idempotency has to survive
options: extend the lease from inside the handler (heartbeat), raise the lease toward the p99 duration, or split the job
a long lease costs redelivery latency when a worker really does die; the queue cannot tell slow from dead

questions.prompt: You need a nightly digest and you run three replicas. Why is `time.Ticker` in the process wrong, and what would you do instead?
expected_points: three replicas means three digests, and zero on a night the ticking replica is restarting
an external scheduler that only enqueues the job
a leader elected through the database — a lock row or a schedules row claimed with a conditional update
idempotent scheduling: derive the job id from the tick so duplicate enqueues collide on the primary key
